sections.title: People & Politics
sections.description: Important developments in governments, societies and the people shaping the world.

cards.title: Hasan Seeks Halt to Execution, Citing Constitutional Violations
cards.content: Nidal Hasan, the former US Army major convicted of the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting that killed 13 people and wounded 32, is asking a judge to halt his execution by firing squad scheduled for December 3. His attorneys filed a motion in US District Court in Kansas, citing constitutional violations and seeking a stay of execution to mount a legal challenge. The motion also seeks to raise habeas corpus, a legal principle that allows individuals to petition for their release if they believe they are being unlawfully detained or imprisoned. A hearing on the matter is set for Wednesday afternoon. Hasan's execution would be the US Army's first since World War II and its first imposition of the death penalty on an armed service member in 65 years.

cards.title: North Korea's Defectors Share Secret Prayer and Persecution Stories
cards.content: North Korean defectors, including Kim Bo-bin, shared their experiences of secret prayer and persecution in a new report by Korea Future. The report documents the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom say they faced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution. The report accuses the regime of violating religious freedom through surveillance, fear, and violence. Kim Bo-bin, who fled 15 years ago, had to be secretive about her Christian faith in North Korea, where unauthorized displays of faith could land people in prison. The report suggests that little has changed despite international pressure, with incidents of suspected Christians being beaten and tortured as recently as last year. North Korea maintains that it allows religious freedom, but rights groups and the United Nations have documented evidence of widespread persecution and control over religion. The report highlights the regime's fear of religious freedom threatening its authority and its efforts to control citizens' beliefs from cradle to grave.

cards.title: Kilmar Ábrego García heads to Spain, ending deportation battle
cards.content: Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national who was wrongfully deported from the US to El Salvador and then returned to the US, is set to leave the country for Spain. García's deportation and subsequent return sparked a bitter debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda. He was arrested in 2019 and initially granted protection from deportation, but was deported in 2025 after the Trump administration intervened. A US judge later ordered his return, and García was eventually released after the charges against him were dropped. Despite initially agreeing to be deported to Costa Rica, García has now chosen to leave the US for Spain, bringing an end to the long-standing deportation battle.

sections.title: Science and technology
sections.description: Discover breakthroughs in science, space, computing and emerging technology.

cards.title: Scientists Uncover Key Mechanism for Protein Linked to Childhood Epilepsy
cards.content: Scientists at the University of Liverpool have discovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that helps position a protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy, CDKL5, within nerve cells. This discovery suggests that some neurological disorders, including CDKL5 deficiency disorder, may arise not only from impaired protein activity but also from proteins failing to reach the locations where they are needed. The researchers found that a single change in the protein can dramatically alter where it resides inside nerve cells, and that mechanical forces generated within cells may help regulate where CDKL5 carries out its biological functions. The findings open up a potential avenue for therapeutic research and offer new hope for improving the lives of children with CDKL5 deficiency disorder.

cards.title: Signal Blocks Screenshots to Protect User Data from AI Agents
cards.content: The privacy-focused messaging app Signal is strengthening its defenses against artificial intelligence agents that can access information on users' screens. The company is blocking screenshots in its iOS app and enabling screen security on Android when an AI assistant tries to read the screen. Signal's move comes amid a broader push by companies to limit or block AI agents over security and customer-protection concerns. The app's president, Meredith Whittaker, emphasized that lack of robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy is a serious problem. Signal's latest move adds to its efforts to limit AI access, including restrictions against Microsoft's Recall AI on Windows 11. The company warned that AI agents can still access private app content through permissions granted during setup. According to AvePoint's State of AI 2026 report, 88.4% of surveyed organizations had experienced at least one AI-agent-related security breach in the previous year. Other companies, including banks and airlines, are also restricting AI agents to protect customer information.

cards.title: CMF Foam Boosts Crash Protection in Cars by Up to 94%
cards.content: A team of researchers has found that replacing conventional front rails in cars with a lightweight metal foam called composite metal foam (CMF) could significantly improve crash protection. The foam, which contains hollow metal spheres embedded in a metallic matrix, absorbs impact energy more effectively than two common designs used in modern vehicles. Simulations showed that CMF rails could reduce maximum deceleration by 38-84%, overall crash severity by 45-94%, and the likelihood of serious head injury by 45-83%. The material's unique structure allows it to withstand substantial compression and impact, making it a promising solution for improving driver and passenger safety. The researchers are now working with manufacturers to explore the potential applications of CMF in vehicles, including electric vehicles, where it could also protect high-voltage battery packs from damage during collisions.

sections.title: Health & wellness
sections.description: Medical research, public health and discoveries that affect everyday wellbeing.

cards.title: Frequent Short Walks Boost Blood Sugar Control, Study Shows
cards.content: Scientists have discovered that taking frequent short walks throughout the day can improve blood sugar control, particularly for people at risk of type 2 diabetes. In a study, participants were assigned to either walk for 45 minutes once a day or in 5-minute breaks throughout the day. The group that took frequent breaks saw a significant increase in time spent within a target blood sugar range, from 82% to 94%, whereas the group that walked in one continuous session experienced a decline. The study suggests that distributing physical activity throughout the day may be as important as the total amount of exercise, and that interrupting prolonged sitting with short walks may offer additional benefits for glucose regulation.

cards.title: CP research challenges previous findings, suggests complex condition
cards.content: New research on cerebral palsy (CP) challenges previous findings and proposes a different understanding of the condition. The study, published in the American Journal of Human Genetics, found that only 89 out of 515 previously linked genes showed a statistically significant association with CP. The researchers suggest that CP may not be a single disease, but rather a collection of symptoms arising from multiple underlying conditions. They propose a 'phenotypic paradigm' for understanding CP, considering it a clinical characteristic that can emerge from different genetic disorders and environmental influences. The study's findings do not disprove connections between CP and other genes, but rather highlight the need for further research and validation before these findings can be applied to patient care.

sections.title: Environment
sections.description: Climate, oceans, ecosystems and the changing planet around us.

cards.title: Global Treaty Proposed to Protect Soil, Citing Risk to $44 Trillion Annual Output
cards.content: Scientists argue that protecting soil requires countries to look beyond their borders, as the thin layer of soil covering Earth's surface is crucial for nourishing ecosystems, filtering water, and supporting life. Despite its importance, soil lacks a dedicated international treaty, with estimates suggesting up to 40 percent of the world's land is already degraded, putting $44 trillion in annual economic output at risk. A proposal for international protection is taking shape, with the University of Sydney's Aroura think tank outlining an eight-stage pathway towards a Global Convention to Secure Soil, targeting adoption in 2032. The authors argue that soil security cannot be achieved by countries acting independently, and that international cooperation is needed to match the scale of the problem, citing the example of ocean governance.

cards.title: Human metabolism's carbon dioxide emissions rise 74% in 30 years
cards.content: A new study by the University of Bath has found that the amount of carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism has increased by 74% over the past three decades, with the global total reaching an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons annually by 2015. The study, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, analyzed thousands of real-world measurements of CO2 production in people of all ages and found that the increase is mainly due to population growth, with more than 60% of the rise attributed to an increase in the number of people rather than a significant change in the amount produced by each individual. The researchers suggest that accounting for this activity could help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be.

cards.title: Srinagar's Water Crisis Worsens due to Climate Change
cards.content: In Srinagar, a water crisis has been ongoing for years, causing daily struggles for residents like Mehak and Zamrood. The absence of a regular water supply has led to the installation of tanks and a hand pump at their homes. Climate change is affecting Doodh Ganga, a vital source of drinking water, causing erratic water supply, low flow, and dry taps. The river's water availability is decreasing due to rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and declining snowmelt. The Kashmir Valley's 24 watersheds, including Doodh Ganga, are experiencing similar impacts.

sections.title: Entertainment
sections.description: Stories from film, music, sports, culture and the world of entertainment.

cards.title: Seven Aspiring Musicians Chosen for Peter Gabriel's Real World Studios Recording
cards.content:
>

The West Country, home to seven aspiring musicians, has been given a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to record at Peter Gabriel's famous Real World Studios in Wiltshire. The seven unsigned bands were selected from over 400 applicants and will follow in the footsteps of acts like Harry Styles, Coldplay, and Amy Winehouse. For many of the musicians, this is their first time recording in a professional studio, and they will leave with a fully mixed and mastered EP. The artists, who are mostly students, face challenges balancing music with work, study, and rising living costs. The chance to record at Real World Studios is a huge privilege and a chance to showcase their talent, with some artists likening it to a dream come true. The initiative aims to provide opportunities to artists outside major music hubs and make a significant difference to their careers. The selected artists, including 1000 Legs, Aloka Collister, and more, are thrilled about the opportunity and look forward to the chance to record and produce high-quality music. The Real World Studios partnership with Arts Council England has given these aspiring musicians the chance to follow their dreams and take their music to the next level. It is a chance for them to showcase their talent, get heard, and make a name for themselves in the music industry. It is an incredible opportunity that will give these artists the chance to work in a world-class studio with the best equipment and professionals in the industry. }

cards.title: Netflix and BBC Launch CBeebies Hub with 24 Shows
cards.content: The BBC and Netflix are launching a trial hub on Netflix featuring 24 CBeebies shows, including popular programmes like Hey Duggee and Teletubbies. The hub, available from December 2, aims to test new ways for the pre-school channel to reach audiences. The BBC will remain the home for all CBeebies content on BBC iPlayer, while some shows like Shaun the Sheep are already available on Netflix. The trial does not include China and will also see Netflix funding a small number of new CBeebies commissions. The partnership aims to drive investment into children's content in the UK and provide a curated selection of CBeebies programmes on Netflix.

cards.title: Children's Booker Prize Shortlists Eight Young Reader Books
cards.content: The first Children's Booker Prize has announced its shortlist of eight books, featuring novels, graphic novels, and an illustrated collection of short stories. The prize is aiming to promote reading among children aged 8-12. A new judging panel, including four child judges, including 12-year-old Ibrahim, will decide the winner. Ibrahim, who was chosen from over 4,000 entrants, is excited to be a part of the process. The shortlisted books are from the UK, Ireland, Australia, and Italy, and the judges are looking for books that convey hope and have different perspectives.

sections.title: economy
sections.description: Markets, businesses, trade and economic changes shaping the global economy.

cards.title: Huawei Found Guilty of Trade Secrets and Fraud
cards.content: A US court has found Huawei guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but acquitted the Chinese technology giant of a more serious racketeering charge. Prosecutors accused Huawei of lying, cheating, and stealing to gain a competitive advantage, but the company's defence team argued that its success was due to its own innovation. Huawei was found guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, including conspiracy to violate US sanctions, but was cleared of the racketeering conspiracy charge. The company's defence team has vowed to defend Huawei's rights and interests, and has already indicated plans to appeal the verdict.

cards.title: UK Energy Bills Rise 26% in January, Typical Bill £2,166
cards.content: Domestic energy bills are expected to rise by 26% in January, according to Cornwall Insight, with a typical annual bill increasing by £443 to £2,166. This is due to Ofgem's new cap, which sets a maximum price for each unit of energy. The rise is expected to be particularly felt by households on variable energy tariffs, with a £37 monthly increase from January to March. The UK government has announced a £100 payment to help households cover winter costs, and a VAT cut on electricity. However, charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and more people to seek emergency support, with Citizens Advice warning that millions of households are entering the coldest months with nothing left. Wholesale gas prices are the dominant driver of the forecast higher prices, with the war in Iran contributing to the increase.

cards.title: Compass Group shifts UK listing to US stock market
cards.content: Catering giant Compass Group is planning to shift its primary stock market listing from the UK to the US, a move that will impact the London Stock Exchange. According to a source close to the company, the official announcement is expected to be made in the company's full-year results on Tuesday. Compass Group operates several brands that provide food and drink services to various places, such as football stadiums, universities, and corporations. The company's decision to list its shares on the US market is reportedly due to the growing number of investors and increasing business it has across the Atlantic, with North America accounting for two-thirds of its business. The move would follow several other UK-based companies that have left the UK to list their shares in the US, including tech firm Arm Holdings and pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca. The decision is expected to have no impact on the number of UK employees and Compass Group will likely retain a secondary listing in London.
